old: And since Dawson doesn't mind riding on top
new: And since my maid Dawson doesn't mind riding up on the coachman's box
reason: Dawson has not been introduced; readers will not know this is Lady Catherine's maid, or what 'riding on top' of the carriage means.
lead_note: Identifies Dawson and the barouche-box briefly, in Lady Catherine's voice

old: by restoring Bingley to all her former good opinion
new: by restoring Bingley to all of Elizabeth's former good opinion
reason: The sentence is about Jane, so 'her' reads as Jane's good opinion, but it means Elizabeth's.
lead_note: Referent made explicit; the source's 'her' means Elizabeth

old: must make her feel the grateful one
new: must make _her_ the one who felt obliged
reason: Stitched-together phrasing; the clause does not clearly say that it is Elizabeth who ought to be thanking the Collinses.
lead_note: Restores the source's emphasis (_her_) and 'obliged' in grammatical form

old: Mr. Bennet said voluntarily to Elizabeth
new: Mr. Bennet said to Elizabeth, quite unprompted
reason: 'Voluntarily' in this sense is dated and reads oddly; the point is that the undemonstrative Mr. Bennet said it unprompted.
lead_note: 'Voluntarily' means unprompted, as the source intends

reason: 'Carsick' is a motor-age word and jars in a horse-drawn carriage.
lead_note: Removes the anachronism; this is the source's own wording

old: Never in her life had she seen his manners so little dignified
new: Never in her life had she seen his manners so unassuming
reason: To a modern reader 'so little dignified' sounds like a criticism (undignified), whereas the point is that he was far less stiff and lofty than usual.
lead_note: 'So little dignified' meant so little lofty; the fix avoids a modern misreading as criticism

old: Elizabeth had assumed that Mr. Darcy would bring his sister to visit her the day after she arrived at Pemberley
new: Elizabeth had assumed that Mr. Darcy would bring his sister to visit her the day after Miss Darcy reached Pemberley
reason: 'She' reads as Elizabeth, who has not arrived at Pemberley; it means Miss Darcy (confirmed in 44.16). The opening sentence of the chapter thus misleads.
lead_note: Referent made explicit (Miss Darcy); matches the source's 'her reaching Pemberley'

old: While these newly formed ideas were forming in their heads
new: While these new ideas were taking shape in their minds
reason: Redundant 'newly formed ... forming' reads like an editing slip.

old: Nothing passed between them that could justify his sister's hopes.
new: Nothing passed between them that could justify Miss Bingley's hopes.
reason: In a sentence about Bingley and Miss Darcy, 'his sister' could be read as Darcy's sister (Miss Darcy herself); it means Miss Bingley.

old: and it was now heightened into something friendlier by the testimony so strongly in his favor, casting his character in such a good light, that yesterday had produced
new: and it was now warmed into something friendlier by yesterday's testimony, which had shown his character in so good a light
reason: The relative clause 'that yesterday had produced' is separated from 'testimony' by a long interruption, so the reader has to re-read to connect them.

old: because of the very wish Elizabeth had long ago attributed to him: that they might one day become his sister's own
new: because of the very wish Elizabeth had long ago attributed to him: that his sister might one day marry into that family
reason: 'That they might one day become his sister's own' is opaque; readers must work out that it means Georgiana marrying into Bingley's family.
lead_note: The source's 'their becoming hereafter her own' made clear

old: His choice is at least disinterested
new: His choice is at least not mercenary
reason: Many readers take 'disinterested' to mean 'uninterested'; here it means he is not marrying for money, which is the point of the sentence.
lead_note: 'Disinterested' here means not marrying for money; clarified

old: for there they switched from their hired carriage to a hackney coach
new: for there they switched from their hired carriage to a hackney coach—a London cab—
reason: 'Hackney coach' is unfamiliar, and the distinction matters to the plot (it signals London, not Scotland); 'turnpikes' in the same letter is also opaque.
lead_note: Brief gloss; the plot depends on it

old: and Mr. Gardiner, having settled the account at the inn, there was nothing left but to go
new: and once Mr. Gardiner had settled the account at the inn, there was nothing left but to go
reason: The sentence switches subject midway and is ungrammatical.

old: "But can you believe Lydia is so lost to everything but her feelings for him
new: "But can you believe," said her aunt, "that Lydia is so lost to everything but her feelings for him
reason: Unattributed; it follows a long speech by Elizabeth and precedes 'replied Elizabeth', so it must be Mrs. Gardiner, but the reader has to infer that.
lead_note: Speaker tag added; the alternation makes it Mrs. Gardiner (the next line is 'replied Elizabeth')

old: for what good would it apparently do anyone
new: for what good could it do anyone
reason: 'Apparently' makes no sense here and reads as a slip.
lead_note: Slip removed; source 'what good could it do'

old: that in Lydia's last letter she had been prepared for something like this
new: that Lydia's last letter had prepared her for something like this
reason: 'She' reads as Lydia; it means Kitty, who had been prepared by Lydia's letter.

old: If he could somehow discover which house the coachman had previously dropped off his fare at, he intended to investigate there, hoping he might find the stand and number of the coach.
new: If he could find out where the coachman had set down his earlier passenger, he meant to ask there, in the hope of learning the coach's number and the cab rank it worked from.
reason: The chain of reasoning (which fare, which house, 'stand and number') is hard to follow, and 'stand' (cab rank) is unfamiliar.
lead_note: Untangled; 'stand' glossed as the cab rank
